title: Dense vs sparse retrieval: how they differ in RAG
description: How dense and sparse retrieval differ in RAG: BM25 versus vector search, hybrid fusion with RRF, the metrics to track, and notes for Vietnamese content.
author: Cross Tech Edu
cover_alt: Flat diagram comparing the sparse and dense retrieval paths in a RAG pipeline
body: **Dense retrieval** embeds text into vectors and compares meaning; **sparse retrieval** matches keywords with BM25. Both find relevant passages in RAG, but they win on different questions: dense for paraphrases, sparse for exact codes and rare terms. The two differ in one fundamental way: what a document looks like when it sits in the index. If the retrieval step is still fuzzy for you, start with [a practical RAG guide for small business](/en/blog/what-is-rag/) and come back here for the internals. ## What is sparse retrieval? **Sparse retrieval** reduces a document to a **bag of words**: a list of terms with their frequencies, with word order and grammar thrown away. The vector is sparse because most dimensions are zero. To search fast, systems build an **inverted index** — a lookup table from each term to the list of documents containing it. A query is split into terms, each term is looked up, and the matching documents are scored. The classic scoring function is **TF-IDF**: term frequency multiplied by inverse document frequency. The modern standard is **BM25**, which adds three refinements: saturated term frequency, inverse document frequency weighting, and length normalization. **Strengths:** - **Exact matching.** Contract codes, invoice numbers, and product SKUs only surface when the exact string is compared. - **Explainable.** You can point at the keyword that made a document match. - **Cheap and fast.** No model, no GPU, and new documents enter the index immediately. **Weaknesses:** - **No sense of meaning.** A question about how long a customer has to send an item back misses a passage titled return window — no content word is shared. - **Stop words add noise.** Words such as `the` or `is` appear everywhere and dilute the score. - **Synonyms need hand-written lists.** You must map buy to purchase yourself. ## What is dense retrieval? **Dense retrieval** does not count words. It embeds text into a fixed-length vector — usually 384, 768, or 1024 dimensions. A **bi-encoder** embeds the question and the document independently with the same weights; the [SBERT paper on arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.10084) is the usual reference point. Document vectors live in a **vector database**. The question is embedded too, then the nearest vectors are found. Brute-force scanning is too slow for large collections, so approximate nearest neighbour search (ANN) structures like **HNSW** or **IVF** trade a little accuracy for a lot of speed. **Strengths:** - **Understands meaning.** Buy and purchase land close together in vector space even without a shared token. - **Handles paraphrase.** A question phrased five different ways returns the same passage. - **Better across languages.** Multilingual models place a Vietnamese question and an English document in one space. **Weaknesses:** - **Codes and numbers are near-noise.** A string such as INV-2026-118 produces no meaningful signal, so dense retrieval often misses exact identifiers. - **More expensive.** You pay for the embedding model, the vector store, and re-embedding the corpus whenever the model changes. - **Hard to explain.** A score is just a distance between vectors; it does not say which term carried the match. ## Side-by-side comparison | Criterion | Sparse retrieval | Dense retrieval | | --- | --- | --- | | Representation | Bag of words with counts | Dense embedding vector | | Matching | Literal term overlap | Semantic, vector distance | | Synonyms | Must be declared by hand | Handled if the model is good | | Codes and exact numbers | Excellent | Weak, often missed | | Cost and latency | Cheap, fast, no GPU | Higher: model, vector store, ANN | | Index updates | New documents searchable immediately, no re-embedding | Must embed new documents; a model change requires a full re-index | | Explainability | You can name the term that matched | Hard; only a vector distance | | Multilingual | Weak without normalization or a dictionary | Strong with a multilingual model | ## Where BM25 still wins **First: saturated term frequency.** A term appearing ten times does not mean a document is ten times more relevant than one where it appears once. BM25 compresses that growth with a logarithmic function. **Second: inverse document frequency weighting.** Agreement appears in every file and separates nothing; INV-2026-118 appears in one document and is therefore extremely precious. **Third: length normalization.** Longer documents have more chances to match a query term, so BM25 applies a correction factor to keep them from dominating every ranking. The [Okapi BM25 formula on Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okapi_BM25) documents each component in detail. ## Why hybrid wins in practice Pick one method and you lose on a specific class of questions. Pick both and fuse the results — that is **hybrid retrieval**. The most common fusion method is **RRF** (Reciprocal Rank Fusion): each document scores by summing 1/(k + rank) across the two lists, with k commonly set to 60. RRF only needs ranks, so it sidesteps the problem of BM25 scores and cosine scores living on different scales. The alternative is a **weighted sum**: the final score equals alpha times the BM25 score plus beta times the cosine score. That is clearer, but alpha and beta need tuning on real questions. After fusion, add a **reranking** step: a heavier model scores each question-passage pair, which is slower but far more accurate, and only then is the top-k cut for the prompt. Dense retrieval also improves before the search starts: [how HyDE works in RAG](/en/blog/what-is-hyde/) has the model write a hypothetical passage first and embeds that instead of the raw question. ## Which one fits your collection - **Codes, SKUs, contract clauses, invoice numbers** → sparse. - **Natural questions and paraphrases** → dense. - **A mix of both kinds of question** → hybrid, and it should be your default. - **A very small corpus, a few dozen files** → build nothing. Put the documents straight into the prompt. - **Several languages in one collection** → dense with a multilingual model, plus sparse to keep identifiers intact. If you would rather have it built, [our software development team](/en/#services) designs, builds and runs RAG systems. ## Measuring and operating it Pick a method with evidence, not with taste. Build a golden set of 20–50 real questions, each with the passage that answers it, and measure: - **recall@k**: does the correct passage appear in the top k? RAG can only use what retrieval surfaces. - **nDCG**: how highly is the correct passage ranked? It separates found it from found it first. - **Latency and cost**: measure query embedding separately from the search itself. - **Index freshness**: how long before a new document shows up in results. Three operating rules apply to both sides: - **Chunking affects both.** Chunks that are too small lose context; chunks that are too large mix topics. Split on sentence boundaries and overlap by 10–15%. - **Use the same embedding model for indexing and querying.** Changing the model without re-indexing fails silently: no error, just bad answers. - **Normalize vectors (L2)** before using dot product so the score is cosine similarity; otherwise vectors with a larger norm dominate. ## Notes for Vietnamese content - **Diacritics matter.** Đổi trả and doi tra are different strings, and BM25 will not know they are the same. Strip diacritics on both index and query side, keeping the original for display. - **Tokenization decides BM25 quality.** Splitting on whitespace performs far worse than a diacritic-aware tokenizer; LLM subword tokenizers shred keywords and blur the score. - **Use a multilingual embedding model, not an English-only one.** English-trained models are noticeably weaker on Vietnamese; index with the same model you serve queries with. - **Write synonym pairs by hand.** Map đổi trả to hoàn hàng and hủy đơn to huỷ đơn, then feed the variants into query expansion or the index. - **Re-measure on Vietnamese questions.** An English golden set tells you nothing about a Vietnamese corpus. ## Frequently asked questions ### Does dense retrieval replace BM25? Not entirely. Dense retrieval wins on paraphrase; BM25 wins on identifiers and rare terminology. If you can only ship one, start with BM25: it is cheaper and easier to operate. ### Do I need a separate vector database? Not necessarily. With a few thousand chunks, an in-process vector index is enough, and most AI platforms include a hosted vector store. Consider a dedicated store when the corpus is large, when many people query at once, or when you need predictable latency. ### Is sparse retrieval just keyword search? Close, but the terms describe different layers. Sparse retrieval is a representation: text becomes a sparse term vector. Keyword search is an application built on that representation. BM25 is one specific scoring function for sparse retrieval, not a complete search system. The shared limit: neither understands meaning, so a question about sending an item back still misses a passage titled return window. ## Conclusion Sparse retrieval counts words, dense retrieval measures meaning, and real RAG systems use both. Starting out: build BM25 first because it is nearly free; add the dense branch when paraphrased questions start to fall through; fuse with RRF and rerank the top results; then measure with your own golden set. If you would rather not build any of it, [our roundup of free AI tools for small business](/en/blog/free-ai-tools-for-small-business/) has ready-made options.
